response: ## The finding `crime_00037` — **Oversized Raster** (`oversized_raster`), `src/assets/hero-banner.png`, severity **low**, confidence **0.95**. Evidence, verbatim: > - `byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB)` > - `severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB` > - `format: png` So: **253.9 KB (260,000 bytes)**, sitting just above the 200 KB low band — a quarter of the way to the 1 MB "high" line. ## Verdict: request changes, don't block The size alone doesn't justify a block. It's the lowest severity band, aggregate `agent_risk` is 0.14 (the second-lowest finding in the whole report), and `effort` is `quick` — this is a five-minute fix that doesn't need to gate a merge. But it shouldn't merge as-is either, for a reason the severity score understates: **this is the landing-page hero**, which means it's almost certainly the LCP element. A 254 KB blocking image on the highest-traffic page has a cost the byte count doesn't capture, and it's the one image on the site where "just under the threshold" is the wrong standard. One honest caveat about the evidence: this finding reports **bytes only** — no dimensions. Contrast `crime_00036`, where the detector had pixel dimensions (`32 × 32 px`) and said so. So crimes is telling you the asset is heavy; it is *not* telling you it's larger than its render area. That part is my inference from "hero banner," and the reviewer should confirm the intrinsic size before prescribing a resize. ## Recommended transformation **Codec first — PNG is the actual bug here.** PNG is lossless and tuned for flat colour and line art. A photographic hero is the worst case for it; that's where most of the 254 KB is going. Even a straight re-encode at the same dimensions should cut 60–80%. **Target dimensions.** A full-bleed hero renders at the viewport width, so there's no single number — ship a `srcset` rather than one file: | Variant | Serves | |---|---| | 768w | mobile 1×, small tablet | | 1280w | laptop 1×, mobile 2× | | 1920w | desktop 1×, laptop 2× | | 2560w (optional) | 2× on wide displays | Cap it at 2560w. Beyond that you're paying real bytes for pixels nobody resolves on a photographic image. Budget **≤100 KB for the 1920w variant** — comfortably achievable in AVIF at q50–60. If the hero is *not* full-bleed (fixed-width card, say 720 CSS px), the whole thing collapses to two files: 720w and 1440w, and you're likely under 40 KB. **WebP vs AVIF: AVIF primary, WebP fallback.** ```html ``` AVIF wins on the specific content type: it's typically 20–50% smaller than WebP at matched perceptual quality on photographic material, and its wider internal bit depth handles the smooth gradients heroes tend to have without the banding WebP's 8-bit 4:2:0 chroma introduces. The costs are encode time (slower, but this is build-time, not request-time) and a support floor of Safari 16.4 / iOS 16.4 — hence the WebP tier underneath, which has been universal since ~2020. **If you can only ship one format, ship WebP.** Universal support, no `` plumbing, still a large win over PNG. AVIF's extra margin isn't worth the fallback complexity on a project that doesn't already have an image pipeline. Two things to add while you're in there, since they're free and this is the LCP element: `fetchpriority="high"` (do *not* lazy-load a hero), and explicit `width`/`height` to reserve layout space and avoid CLS. ## Adjacent, out of scope for this PR Worth flagging to the author but not blocking on: `crime_00032` (`svg_with_embedded_raster`, `src/assets/partner-logo.svg`) is the **high**-severity asset finding in this report — an SVG with two base64 rasters inside it, which is the mime type lying about what it contains. If this PR is touching assets anyway, it's a natural companion cleanup.
